ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Safeguard agreement with IAEA 
*61. SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the draft Bill on the US and India Nuclear Cooperation Promotion Act 
of 2006 states that the US President must first determine that India and the International 
Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) have concluded safeguard agreements requiring the 
application of IAEA safeguards in perpetuity; and 
(b) if so, the reaction of Government on this which runs completely contrary to the 
assurance given by the Prime Minister in both Houses of Parliament that India would 
approach the IAEA for safeguards only after USA endorses the July 18, 2005 
nuclear deal? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS 
(SHRI ANAND SHARMA): (a) and (b) A Statement is placed on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
(a) Section 4(b) (2) of the US House Bill entitled "United States and India Nuclear 
Cooperation Promotion Act of 2006" proposes a Presidential Determination that India and 
IAEA have concluded an agreement requiring the application of IAEA safeguards in 
perpetuity in accordance with IAEA standards, principles, and practices [including IAEA 
Board of Governors Document GOV/1621 (1973)] to India's civil nuclear facilities, 
materials, 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2006] 
and programmes as declared in India's Separation Plan, including material, used in or 
produced through the use of India's civil nuclear facilities. 
(b) The Prime Minister in his statement to Parliament on 29 July, 20 had 
stated that "Before voluntarily plac ing our civilian facilities under IAE 
safeguards, we will ensure that all restrictions on India have been lifted. The 
Government continues to abide by that commitment. Technicai discussions 
have taken place on an India- specific Safeguards Agreement with the IAEA on 8 
July, 2006. But there is no question of pl acing Indian civilian facilities under 
safeguards till we are assured that restrictions on civil nuclear energy 
cooperation with India have been lifted. Further, the Bill reported out by the 
House International Relations Committee is still under consideration, and at this 
stage, it would be difficult to predict the language of the final legislation, 
including any reference to the Safeguards Agreement. 
SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Sir, I have gone through the reply of the 
Government. It is clear that there are wide divergencies existing between the 
position of the Government of India's and the United States of America's law 
makers. In this context, Sir, I would like to further ask whether the IAEA 
safeguards proposed by the two versions of the Bill would be India-specific as 
committed earlier by the Prime Minister or they would be in accordance with 
the modern additional protocols, which are generally perceived as intrusive. 
This is my first question. 
SHRI ANAND SHARMA: Sir, the reply has made the position of the 
Government very clear. For the benefit of this august House and the hon. Member, 
I may mention that India has agreed to  enter into civilian nuclear energy 
cooperation with the United States of America and with other international 
partners. As for the United States of Am erica, July 18 Stat ement by the hon. 
Prime Minister, Dr. Manmohan Singhji and President Bush outlines the 
roadmap. And it also contains reciprocal obligations, the steps to be taken by 
the United States of America and the steps which we have agreed to take. In 
July 18 Statement, what is important is that there is an implict recognition of 
the fact that India has a military nuclear programme and, therefore, calls for a 
separation of civilian and the strategic facilities. That separation plan, we had 
agreed to, was filed in both the Houses of Parliament. It also requires that for the 
civilian nuclear facilities India enters into an agreement with the IAEA. 
2 

[27 July, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
But that agreement would be India-specific. That agreement is required since we did not 
have any of our facilities under the safeguards. Under the same arrangement, even the 
nuclear weapon States have safeguards agreements with the IAEA. It will ensure, Sir, a multi-
layer supply of reliable uninterrupted fuel of India. There is an interlocking mechanism 
when we talk about safeguards. It is not only uninterrupted fuel supply but it will also 
allow India to build up a strategic reserve and also to take corrective measures which we 
may need by approaching other fuel suppliers and other countries if the situation were to 
demand so. Sir, it is only placing our civilian facilities under IAEA and I repeat only 
the civilian facilities, since the military nuclear facilities have been kept out which 
include the power reactors the fast breeder reactors, the prototype fast breeder reactors 
and linking facilities-upstream and downstream. Having said that about the additional 
protocol, an additional protocol will also be signed. With IAEA again that arrangement is 
there also for the other nuclear States. That additional protocol which India will sign will 
not be the same as a non-nuclear weapon State. That I would like to assure the House 
that the discussions are on between India and the IAEA on this safeguards agreement and 
additional protocol in any case would follow after safeguards agreement have 
been concluded.

SHRI MOINUL HASSAN: Sir, my (a) part of my question is: Would the 
Indian civilian nuclear programme come under the IAEA safeguard regime as that 
of a non-nuclear weapon State? My (b) part of my question is: Would the US 
also have the right to send its own weapons inspector? These are my two 
supplementary questions. 
SHRI ANAND SHARMA: Sir, just for the benefit of all the Members of the 
House and also the distinguished former Foreign Minister, Yashwant Sinhaji, I 
would like to say that we are in the process of negotiating with the IAEA an 
India specific safeguards agreement. Secondly, I would also like to make it clear 
that there is an inter-locking mechanism, when we sign the safeguards, which 
will ensure not only fuel stockpiling, as I said, uninterrupted supplies but there 
will also be trilateral agreements which the United State of America will have 
with India and the IAEA. Having said that, with regard to inspections, those will 
be only by the IAEA; the Safeguards Agreements will be with the IAEA and 
only for the civilian facilities. The determination is the sovereign determination 
of India. It is the scientific community which has decided upon the separation 
plan and identified those facilities which are civilian and the other facilities which 
are strategic so that India's strategic programme and the credible minimum 
deterrent is not undermined in any manner. There will not be inspection by any 
other country. It will be with the IAEA. That is what I wanted to say.

the bargain, the U.S. Administration also uses all its influence with the 
American Congress to ensure that what is contemplated is within the 
parameters of July 18 Statement, it is certainly true that in the Bills that were 
before the Committees of the House of Representatives and the Senate, these are 
elements which are of concern to us. And adequte representations have been made 
to the United States Government. And, I spoke to President Bush himself. 
Now, I have an assurance that the United States Administration will do all it can 
to ensure that the parameters, the goal posts of July 18 are not tampered with. 
Now, the US legislative process is still on. The House of Representatives may 
have taken up a Bill. There is the Senate  Bill, and when there is a difference 
between the two Sills, there will be a reconciliation. I cannot say that I can 
predict what will be the end product of U.S. legislative process. All I can say 
is, if the United States legislative process leads to an end product which is not 
consistent with what we have committed, that would be the determining factor 
of what we can do with it.

Sports infrastructure in rural areas 
*62. SHRI SANJAY RAUT: Will the Minister of YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that there is acute shortage of sports infrastructure 
facilities in rural areas; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor and the steps taken to start an effective 
programme for youth of rural areas; and 
(c) the details of the schemes under which financial assistance is provide 
for the promotion of sports in the country through NGOs and performance 
review of such schemes, particularly in Maharashtra State? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ AND YOUTH AFFAIRS AND 
SPORTS (SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR): (a) to (c) A Statement is laid on 
the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) As 'Sports' is & State subject in the Constitution, the primary 
responsibility for the creation of sports infrastructure facilities throughout 
17 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2006] 
the country, including the rural areas, falls on State Governments. Till 
31.3.2005, the Ministry was supplementing the efforts of the State 
Governments for the creation of sports facilities in various States by providing 
assistance under the Centrally Sponsored Sports Infrastructure Schemes in 
accordance with the approved pattern subject to the receipt of viable proposals. 
With effect from 1.4.2005 however, the Sports Infrastructure Schemes were 
transferred to the State sector. The fresh cases of Sports Infrastructure projects 
will have to be funded by State Governments out of their own resources. All 
State Governments were informed accord ingly in February , 2005. However, 
the Planning Commission has indicated that funds to the extent of committed 
liabilities will be provided for ongoing approved Sports Infrastructure projects 
during the remaining period of the Tenth Plan only. In recognition of the 
continuing acute, shortage of sports facilities in rural areas, thus denying the vast 
majority of children, adolescents and youth access to organized sports and 
games, consideration is being given to  the promotion of a Panchayat Yuva 
Khel Abhiyan in collaboration with schools and other educational institutions, 
on the one hand, and with Panchayati Raj Institutions, on the other. 
(c) The Ministry is implementing the scheme of Assistance to National Sports 
Federations. Under the scheme, Central assistance is provided to the 
recognized National Sports Federations, which are autonomous registered 
bodies, for purposes such as for participation in tournaments & Training 
abroad, organizing National/International Championships in India and purchase 
of Sports Equipments. These recognized Federations are National level bodies 
which are responsible for promotion of Sports in the country as a whole in 
consultation with their affiliated State Units. Government of India does not deal 
with State Level Sports Federations/ Associations and as such State-wise data 
are not maintained. The performances of the recognised NSFs are reviewed 
from time to time. 
However, details of financial assistance provided to different States during 
the last three years under  the erstwhile Scheme of "Grants for Creation of 
Sports Infrastructure" (including Maharashtra) is enclosed as Statement-I (See 
below). The figures indicated include grants released to NGOs in respective 
States.

Role of Gram Sabhas 
*67. KUMARI NIRMALA DESHPANDE: Will the Minister of 
PANCHAYATI RAJ be pleased to state: 
(a) the role of the Gram Sabhas in implementing various schemes for 
helping the poor; 
28 

[27 July, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) whether it is a fact that Gram Sabhas are being neglected and not 
encouraged to function; and 
(c) if so, the remedial measures planned to make the Gram Sabhas 
effective? 
THE MINISTER OF PANCHAYATI RAJ (SHRI MANI SHANKAR 
AIYAR): (a) to (c) Statement is laid on the Table of the House. 
Statement 
(a) to (c) Article 243-A of the Constitution provides for the establishment of 
Gram Sabhas to "exercise such powers and perform such functions at the 
village level as the Legislature of a State may, by law provide". During the 
first Round Table of State Ministers of Panchayti Raj held in Kolkata in July 
2004, it was decided that State Governments may review the extant legislation to 
determine the legislative and other steps needed to be taken to ensure that the 
powers and functions mentioned in Article 243 A are adequately incorporated in 
the State legislation. These include constitution of Sabhas below the Gram level 
such as Gram Sansad of Ward Sabha, Periodicity of meetings of Gram Sabhas 
and Ward Sabhas and empowering the Gr am Sabha with measures such as 
right to all information required to make the Panchayats truly answerable to 
the Gram Sabha, approval of plans prepared by the Gram Panchayat, issue of 
utilization certificates of funds allocated for the plans, programmes of the 
Panchayat and identification of beneficiaries. 
The Ministry is aware that the Gram Sabhas do not function as 
effectively as they ought to function. The Ministry is taking several steps to 
remedy the situation and to establish the Gram Sabha as the bedrock of true 
decentralization. Some of these steps are listed below: 
   An Expert Group constituted by the Ministry of Panchayati Raj on 
planning at the grass roots level has submitted its report in March 
2006 which has been accepted by the Ministry. Some of the 
recommendations of the Group relate to participative planning at 
the Gram Panchayat level and it has been suggested in this context that 
certain steps should be carried out  on a campaign mode to ensure 
good participation in Gram Sabhas and Ward Sabhas. These include 
advance notice of meetings, mobilization of special interest 
29 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2006] 
groups such as self-help groups for attending the Ward and Gram Sabhas, 
compaigns through National Survey Scheme and Nehru Yuvak Kendra 
Volunteers, nomination of facilitators for each Ward Sabha and having a 
proper structure for the Gram and Ward Sabha with scope to break up into 
smaller groups for discussion. 
 While reviewing the Centrally Sponsored Schemes of various 
Ministries, the Ministry of Pancha yati Raj, is insisting that the 
Gram Sabha should have a major role to play in selection of 
beneficiaries and works, monitoring of programmes and approving 
the utilization certificates etc. 
 With a view to interacting with Panchayats and carryingout a review 
with the authorities concerned of the progress in implementing the 
points for action mutually agreed upon in the round Tables, a process 
of visiting the States and UTs at the level of Union Minister of 
Panchayati Raj has also been initiated. The Minister has so far 
visited fourteen States and two UTs, namely, Karnataka, West 
Bengal, Uttaranchal, Haryana, Chhattisgarh, Orissa, Arunachal 
Pradesh, Rajasthan, Sikkim, Goa, Andhra Pradesh, Punjab, 
Himachal Pradesh, Kerala, Chandigarh and Lakshadweep. Each 
visit is concluded with a Statement of Conclusions jointly signed 
with the Chief Minister of the State concerned, highlighting the 
key points of action on which the State would move to 
operationalise the recommendations of the round Tables. In the 
case of Kerala, the Statement has been initialed by the Union 
Minister of Panchayati Raj and the Minister for Local Self 
Government, Kerala. It is expected that the Chief Minister will sign 
the approved version of the Joint Statement on his next visit to 
Delhi, as was the case with Chief Minister of Sikkim. The role of 
Gram Sabha is being emphasized in all the Joint Statements. 
 In 2006-07, the Ministry of Panchayati Raj is implementing the 
Panchayat Empowerment and Incentive Scheme. Under the scheme, 
grants wit be released to State Governments only when they agree to 
give a commitment to undertake reforms through a Joint Statement 
or Agreement with Ministry of Panchayati Raj. One of the reform 
areas taken into consideration in the scheme is assigning powers to 
30 

[27 July, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
the Gram Sabhas to approve plans, select beneficiaries, authorize 
utilization certificates, be consulted for land alienation etc., and to 
ensure that the meetings are conducted with due procedure. 
 The Ministry would also be implementing the scheme of Rashtriya 
Gram Swaraj Yojana in the current year. One of the components of 
the schemes is providing of training to elected representatives and 
officials of Panchayati Raj Institutions. Through this scheme also 
efforts will be made to make the Gram Panchayats fully accountable to 
the Gram Sabhas. 
 The legislative provisions relating to the Constitutions/quorum etc. 
of Gram Sabhas in different States are also being examined and the 
States are being continually advised to amend the provisions so as 
to make the Gram Sabhas hold the Panchayats accountable as well 
as to carry out social audit. In this connection, UNDP has funded a 
Study on Jurisprudence of Panchayati Raj Institutions which was 
implemented by two NGOs viz., the Rural Litigation and 
Entitlement Kendra (RLEK), Dehradun and the Institute of Social 
Studies (ISS), New Delhi. The st udy covers all the States and 
inter-alia, had analyze the State Panchayati Raj Acts, status of 
decentralization and progressive judgements related to Panchayats. One 
of the focal points was the powers granted to the Gram Sabhas in the 
State acts. The study has been completed and the final reports are being 
examined by the Task Force on Jurisprudence. Comments of the States 
have also been invited before further action is initiated on the 
recommendations. 
 Under the Panchayats (Extension to the Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996 
(PESA) which extends Panchayati Raj to Fifth Schedule areas in 
nine States of Andhra Pradesh, Chhatisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal 
Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Prad esh, Maharashtra, Orissa and 
Rajasthan, Gram Sabhas have b een given special powers. These 
include the power to approve the plans, programmes and projects 
for social and economic development before such plans, 
programmes and projects are taken up for implementation by the 
Panchayat at the village level; to be responsible for the identification 
or selection of persons as beneficiaries under the poverty alleviation 
and other programmes; to certify the utilization of funds by the 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2006] 
Panchayats and to safeguard and preserve the traditions and customs of the 
the people, their cultural identity, community resources and the customary 
mode of dispute resolution. The Ministry is taking several steps to implement 
the provisions of PESA in letter and spirit so that the institution of Gram 
Sabhas is strengthened. 
KUMARI NIRMALA DESHPANDE: Sir, there are various schemes, 
projects for the betterment of the poor but the major problem is of proper 
implementationl The best guarantee would be the Gram Sabha, which is formed 
by all the adult members of the village community. So, if they are made active, 
and if they can take the decisions, monitor the projects, monitor all the 
schemes, then we will have proper implementation. But it is found that nobody 
is interested in mobilizing the people and making the Gram Sabha active. 
How can that be done? 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, I entirely agree with the Hon. 
Member that the Gram Sabha is the fulcrum around which an effective 
Panchayati Raj system must revolve. And, to this end, I am glad to inform the 
hon. Member that a large number of States have, in fact, in recent times, taken 
steps to empower the Gram Sabhas, to authorise them to look into matters that 
would make meetings of the Gram Sabha relevant and meaningful, and that there 
is a continuing dialogue between the Union Government and the State 
Governments in this regard reflected in the conclusions on the issue of the 
Gram Sabha during the Seven Round Tables that were held in 2004 and 
which continue to figure in the tours that I have been undertaking of States and 
Union Territories. Thus far I have visited 15 States and 2 Union Territories. And, 
with each of them we have entered into a kind of Memorandum of 
Understanding or a joint statement on co nclusions where issues relevant to 
the Gram Sabhas are raised wherever both the sides believe that something 
needs to be stressed. This is work in progress and we do need to make the 
Gram Sabhas more active. To this end, NGOs, such as the ones that the hon. 
Member has said runs, could play an in valuable role in mobilizing people to 
attend these meetings. I must say that once any State decides to also subsidiary 
sabhas at the ward level, the degree of attendance and participation have 
recorded a sensible increase. 
KUMARI NIRMALA DESHPANDE: Sir, unless it becomes mandatory that 
the meetings of Gram Sabha should take place, the objective of 
32 

[27 July, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
Panchayati Raj, which Gandhiji used to say is gram -swaraj, that will not be 
achieved. It always happens that some functionaries of the Government" and 
some elected representatives together manage many things and that never 
reaches the poor beneficiaries. So, some stricter measures need to be taken. 
SHRI MANI SHANKAR AIYAR: Sir, while agreeing that some stricter 
measures need to be taken, I may also point out that in the case of most, if 
not all State Governments there is a mandatory provision in the State law for 
Gram Sabhas to be convened at regular in tervals. In some States it is twice a 
year; in some other States, it is four tim es a year. But, we cannot compel the 
members of the Gram Sabha to attend a meeting. The one exception that I 
know of is the Jumsas of Sikkim where the local body has itself taken the 
decision that any family whose repres entative does not attend a Gram Sabha 
meeting will be appropriately fined by th at local body. But, this is a decision 
taken locally by the local authority. I would commend the example to Gram 
Sabhas all around the country. But what is required is that greater attention 
should be given through a legal provisions governing the Gram Sabhas and 
that we have agreed to.

Placing of India on "Watch List" by US 
*64. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Annual Report 2006 of the States Department of 
the United States has categorized India as the sources, destination, and transit country for 
men, women and children trafficked for the purposes of forced or bonded labour and 
commercial sexual exploitation and placed our country in the "Watch List"; 
(b) if so, the details of Government's response, if any, conveyed to the US thereto; 
(c) the basis of the said response; and 
(d) the implications of a country being placed in the "Watch-List" by the US 
administration? 
35 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2006] 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI ANAND SHARMA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The Government has noted the US practice of issuing global reports on such 
subjects and stated that such reports by their very nature are based on US view 
points and preconceptions and rejected any judgemental and prescriptive approach 
by a foreign Government. India and US have an ongoing dialogue on the subject 
of trafficking in persons and other transnational challenges and the approach of the 
2006 report does not reflect the active cooperation on this subject between the 
two countries and is certainly not helpful to furthering our dialogue in this 
regard. 
(c) The Government is of the opinion that there is sufficient recognition within 
India of the problem of trafficking. An elaborate mechanism of constitutional 
and other laws and regulations, an independent judiciary and free media exist 
within the country for the redressal of the problem. The Government is also 
currently considering additional steps to deal with this problem, including 
cooperating with other countries,. It does not consider that a judgemental and 
prescriptive approach to the problem by a foreign country is helpful in dealing 
with the problem. 
(d) For countries on the Tier 2 "Watch List", the US Secretary of State is 
required to submit to the US Congress, an "interim assessment" of anti-
trafficking efforts of that country in February of each year.

268. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of COAL be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the Committee, headed by T.L. Shankar, set up to 
recommend measures to meet the demand-supply gap and also to examine the 
current policy on captive coal mines etc. has, in the first part of its recent report, 
highlighted, inter-alia, that the country will f ace pronounced coal shortages 
over the next four years and recommended import of high grade thermal coal; 
and 
(b) if so, the details of other major recommendations/observations made by 
the Committee and the action taken/proposed to be taken thereon? 
66 

[27 July, 2006} RAJYA SABHA 
THE  MINISTER OF  STATE  IN  THE MINISTRY OF  COAL (DR. 
DASARI NARAYAN RAO): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) The other major recommendations/observations made by the 
Committee are as follows: 
(i) As coal shall remain India's primary source of commercial energy supply, a 
time bound plan to cover the entire country by regional mapping in 15 years 
should be prepared by Geological Survey of India, Central Mine Planning 
and Design Institute and Ministry of Coal, Government of India. 
(ii) Coal India Limited (CIL) may be granted the status of Navratna company 
and the subsidiaries of CIL may be granted the status of Mini Ratna 
companies in which case only those proposals of such a subsidiary would 
need Government approval wherein the capital expenditure exceeds Rs. 
500 crore. 
(iii) The environmental issue in respect of projects should be taken up on 
priority consideration by the Government. 
(iv) Planned imports of coal needs to be encouraged. 
(v) Increasing proportion of all domestic coal that is not earmarked for 
Power Sector be brought into auction market over the next 2 to 3 
years. 
(vi) The current system of linkages feeding the power sector may be replaced 
with formal long term Fuel Supply and Transport Agreements that 
include the Railways. 
(vii) The procedures and processes need to be streamlined to expedite the 
allotment of the captive coal blocks  in a transparent and effective 
manner. 
(viii) All possible legal measures should be evolved to cancel the licenses 
issues earlier if the allottee has not taken adequate steps to bring the allotted 
mines to production or in setting up the end use units. 
(ix) Coal price would need to be regulated in light of the market realities. 
The regulation of coal price has to be differentiate the pricing of coal 
for power generation since it consumes 80% of 
67

the domestic production and the quality of coal it consumes is not 
easily saleable to the steel and cement sectors. 
(x) The Railway tariff for coal should be subject to a detailed review by an 
independent agency, preferably headed by a High/Supreme Court Judge. 
(xi) The Railways should in consultation with Planning Commission and 
the Ministries of Coal and Power determine the main corridors through 
which coal would move in very large quantities to power plants and 
examine the cost an feasibility of setting up dedicated truck-routes for 
coal transport.

3. Under 'Increasing production through Emergency Coal Production Plan'

E-Governance projects 
270. SHRI MAHENDRA MOHAN: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that recently a detailed plan has been launched for execution of 
26 mission mode E-govemance projects and eight support components at an estimated cost 
of Rs. 23000 crores for creating citizens - centric and business-centric environment for 
governance; 
(b) if so, the details thereof, including the phased programme drawn up for its 
execution; and 
(c) the details of the monitoring machinery set up to ensure time-bound 
implementation of the various projects so that the benefits of information technology 
are available to the citizens as early as possible? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) and (b) Government has approved the National e-
Governance Plan (NeGP) covering its Vision, Approach, 26 Mission Mode projects 
& 8 support components is given in the enclosed statement (See below) Assigning of 
Roles and Responsibilities and Programme Management Structure required for 
Implementation of NeGP. Financial details would need to be worked out project-
wise by the concerned line Ministries/Departments/State Governments and for these 
projects, approval of competent authority would be required as per the existing 
provisions of General Financial Rules. 
NeGP. provides an over-arching framework under which various Mission Mode 
Projects and supporting Components would be executed. Whilst NeGP would be an 
ongoing programme, individual project/ components will have phased plan. 
(c) Apex Committee under the Chairmanship of Cabinet Secretary is overseeing 
the implementation of NeGP programme and a Body under the Chairpersonship of 
Prime Minister would be monitoring the programme. In addition, project level 
monitoring would be carried out by respective line Ministry/Department/State 
Government.

271. SHRIMATI SHOBANA BHARTIA: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased 
to state: 
(a) whether after coming down heavily on telecom operators carrying grey 
international long distance telephone calls, his Ministry has now started to crack down 
on courier companies who are allegedly bringing post from foreign countries into 
the country illegally; 
(b) if so, whether a number of courier companies in the country were bringing in 
huge consignments of post from foreign countries and then injecting into the Indian 
postal network to avoid payment of terminal dues to postal department; and 
(c) if so, the total revenue loss Government suffered and the steps taken to check 
this revenue loss? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) and (b) No, Sir. 
(c) Does not arise in view of (a) and (b) above.

(b) if so, the details thereof; and

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF

Telephone exchanges in Andhra Pradesh 
273. SHRI C. RAMACHANDRAIAH: Will the Minister of 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) the total number of telephone exchanges functioning in Andhra Pradesh 
particularly in Cuddapah district and their exchange-wise capacity as on date: 
(b) whether Government propose to increase the present capacity of the existing 
telephone exchanges and also to open some new telephone exchanges; 
(c) if so, the details of the same; and 
(d) the steps taken/proposed to be taken to exhaust the waiting list in the said 
district? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) the total number of telephone exchanges in Andhra Pradesh is 
3587 and the number of telephone exchanges functioning in Cuddapah District is 129. 
The exchange-wise capacity is given in the enclosed Statement, (See below). 
(b) There is no capacity constraint in any of the exchanges, as such there is no 
proposal for opening new telephone exchanges. 
(c) Does not arise in view of (a) and (b) above. 
(d) The following steps are being taken to exhaust the waiting list: 
(i) Wherever underground cable network exists landline connection are being 
provided. Small lengths of underground cable are also being laid wherever 
necessary. 
(ii) 10 additional WLL Base Transceiver Stations (BTS) with capacity of 9000 lines 
were commissioned in 2005-06. During 1 st quarter of 2006-07, 3 WLL BTSs 
with a capacity of 2250 lines were commissioned. Another WLL BTS of 
750 lines is likely to be commissioned in August, 2006.

Cyber crime 
287. MS. MABEL REBELLO: Will the Minister of COMMUNICATIONS 
AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY be pleased to state: 
(a) the efforts that are being made to  reduce the cyber crime in this 
country; 
(b) whether Government have any proposal to upgrade and educate the 
personnel to combat this menace; and 
(c) the action that has been taken to have a liaison with the counterparts in other 
countries to combat cyber crime? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF 
COMMUNICATIONS AND INFORMATION TECHNOLOGY (DR. 
SHAKEEL AHMAD): (a) and (b) The Government has taken several steps to 
check cyber crimes in the country. Major steps are: 
- A legal framework has been put in  place to handle cyber crime through 
IT Act, 2000. Cyber crimes are ade quately covered under this Act and 
the legislative provisions in this Act are being further strengthened to 
include some of the crimes which were not covered earlier. 
- The Office of Controller of Certifying Authority (CCA) has been set up 
for implementing the provisions of the IT Act, 2000 which provides legal 
recognition for transactions carried out by means of electronic data 
interchange and other means of electronic communications. 
- Information Security is an importa nt area to reduce cyber crime and 
Department of Information Technology (DIT) has initiated Information 
Security Education and Awareness programme (ISEA) for development of 
Human Resource under which awareness and training programmes as 
well as Diploma/Certificate courses are offered through 5 Resource 
Centres and 34 Participating Institutions (IITs, Engineering Colleges, etc). 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2006] 
- DIT is also promoting R&D in information security to help in 
enhancing expertise in surveillance of cyber space and cyber forensics. 
- The Government has conducted several awareness and training 
programmes on cyber laws and cyber crimes for Law Enforcement 
Agencies and Judicial Officers. 
- Central Bureau of Investigation and other Police Organisations have set up 
cyber crime cells and also conduct awareness and training programmes. 
- All the Directorate of Forensic Science Laboratories i.e. CFSLs 
(located at Chandigarh, Kolkata and Hyderabad) and GEQDs (located at 
Shimla, Kolkata and Hyderabad) have computer forensic facility for 
forensic analysis of the cyber crime exhibits and also conduct regular 
training programmes for law enforcement agencies in the field of search 
and seizure of the digital evidence, its handling and the incidence 
response. 
- Indian Computer Emergency Response Team (CERT-ln) has been set up 
to promote cyber security and help organisations recover from computer 
security incidents. CERT-ls has issued a number of Advisories, and 
circulated security guidelines for securing websites to all Government 
organisations and published it on CERT-ln website (http://www/cert-in.org. 
in). CERT-ln also conducts regular security workshops for the system and 
network administrators of the critical information sector organisations. 
(c) CERT-ln regularly interacts with the other CERTs located worldwide to 
handle security incidents. 
Cyber crime cases are covered under Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties 
(MLATs), which we have with various countries. Moreover, India is a 
member of Cyber Crime Technology Information Network System (CTINS), 
which is a Japanese Government initiative for mutual exchange of information 
regarding cyber crimes among the member countries which is advisory in nature. 
This system is presently installed in the Cyber Crime Investigation Branch 
(EOU-IX) of CBI. Cyber Crime Investigation Cell; 
112 

[27 July, 2006] RAJYA SABHA

Legislation to regulate T.V. channels and information media 
334. SHRI MANOHAR JOSHI: Will the Minister of INFORMATION AND 
BROADCASTING be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to enact a legislation to regulate the 
working of T.V. channels and information media; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether Government have taken note of the massive intrusion of media 
in the privacy of individuals and other entities under the facade of investigative 
journalism; and 
(d) if so, the action taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF INFORMATION AND BROADCASTING (SHRI 
PRIYARANJAN DASMUNSI): (a) and (b) The Ministry of Information and 
Broadcasting is considering a proposed Broadcasting Services Regulation Bill 
in consultation with the concerned Ministries. A need has also been felt to 
consult the media in the matter. 
(c) and (d) In so far as the print media are concerned, all such allegations of 
intrusion of the privacy of individuals would be considered by the Press Council 
of India, which is an independent body over which Government does not 
exercise control. Moreover, this issue is regulated on the basis of code of 
journalistic ethics. In so far as electronic media are concerned, such a specific 
code has not been formulated. The Government has set up a committee to 
formulate a programme code based upon the concept of self regulation by TV 
channels.

Status of Ranchi-Vijayawada N.H. 
†368. SHRI RUDRANARAYAN PANY: Will the Minister of SHIPPING, 
ROAD TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS be pleased to state: 
(a) the status of proposed Ranchi-Vijayawada National Highway as on date; 
(b) by when this work is likely to be completed; and 
(c) the approach of Governments of those States towards this project through 
which this highway would be passing? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF SHIPPING, ROAD 
TRANSPORT AND HIGHWAYS (SHRI K.H. MUNIAPPA): (a) to (c) The 
proposal of the Government of Orissa to declare the Ranchi-Vijayawada road as 
National Highway was received but the Planning Commission has suggested to 
develop this route to two-lane highway as an integrated project by the Central and State 
Governments through various available funding options. In this regard, Chief Minister 
of Orissa has forwarded a proposal to the Prime Minister on 12.06.2006 suggesting 
tentative funding options within a time frame of 3 to 4 years and sought formal approval 
of the Central Government. It is too early to indicate the date of completion of this 
mega project. 
Out of the total length of 1673 km, entire length of about 454 km. of this route 
falling in Andhra Pradesh and Jharkhand and about 227 km in Orissa is already 
National Highways. Remaining 992 km is part of state highways and rural roads. 
Central Government is developing these National Highways depending upon traffic 
need and availability of funds.

Sir, I may state here that the expressi on "holds any office of profit under 
the Government" occurring in article 102 of the Constitution has nowhere been 
defind precisely. Its scope has to be gathered from the pronouncements made, 
from time to time, by the Supreme Court and of the High Courts as to what 
constitutes the expressions "office", "profit" and "under the Government." The 
courts are of the view, I again repeat, the courts are of the view that a practical 
view, not pedantic baskets of tests, must guide the courts to arrive at an 
appropriate conclusion whether the concerned office is an "office of profit." 
Sir, article 102(1) (a) of the Consti tution provides that a person shall be 
disqualified for being chosen as, and for be ing, a Member of either House of 
Parliament, if he holds an office of profit under the Government of India or the 
Government of any State, I may here then say, other than office declared by 
Parliament by law not to disqualify its holder. So, it is the Parliament which has 
the power to exempt those Members of Parliament who are holding the office 
of profit. 
The Constitution of India demarcates the legislative powers between the 
Union and States to deal with the disq ualification of Members of Parliament 
and Members of the State Legislatures. The power of the State Legislatures, in 
respect of their members is contained in article 191 (1) (a) of the Constitution 
and, accordingly, State Legislatures have enacted the Prevention of 
Disqualification Acts for their respective States. Any attempt by Parliament to lay 
down generic criteria which will apply to the members of State Assemblies may 
be seen as an encroachment by the Parliament in the domain of State 
Legislatures. 
Sir, the Parliament and State Leg islatures have plenary powers of 
legislation within the fields assigned to them, and subject to certain 
constitutional and judicially recognised restrictions can legislate prospectively 
as well as retrospectively. There is a famous case from Rajasthan in which 
the Supreme Court gave its ruling. The Supreme Court in Kanta Kathuria 
versus Manak Chand AIR 1970 SC 694 held that article 191 of the Constitution 
itself recognises the power of the Legislature of the State to declare by law that 
the holder of an office shall not be

disqualified for being chosen as a Member and for being a member of the 
Legislature. There is nothing in the words of the article to indicate that this 
declaration cannot be made with retrospective effect. The word 'declared' in 
article 191 (1) (a) does not imply any limitation, Sir, I am laying emphasis on 
'limitation on the powers of the legislature.' The declaration can be made 
effective as from an early date. This is the rationale of the law of 1970, 
Supreme Court. 
The Government has, therefore,  carefully and respectfully 
considered the message of the hon. President and it is of the view that the Bill 
should again be considered and passed by the Parliament. 
Sir, I commend the Bill for the consideration of this august House.

STATEMENTY BY PRIME MINISTER 
The situation in Lebanon and Evacuation of Indian Nationals 
THE PRIME MINSTER (DR. MANMOHAN SINGH): Hon. Members are 
aware of the current situation in Lebanon. Taking into account the concern that 
Members may have on this score, I rise to apprise the House of the current 
situation and our responses to the evolvi ng situation, especially the efforts 
made by us to aid and assist Indian nationals who have become victims of the 
escalating crisis in Lebanon 
Sir, West Asia is our extended neighbourhood and tensions in that region 
affect our security and our vital interests. We are seriously concerned about 
the escalation of the conflict between Israel and the Hezbollah extending 
across the Lebanon-Israel border. These developments have inflamed an 
already tense and delicate situation in the region. 
On July 12, India had condemned the the abduction of two Israeli soldiers 
by the Hezbollah cadres and called for their immediate release. Simultaneously, 
we had condemned in the strongest possible terms the 
329 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2006] 
excessive and disproportionate military retaliation by Israel. We had 
particularly expressed concern that the action of the Israeli Defence Forces had 
resulted in killing and suffering of innocent civilians, including women and children, 
that is likely to exacerbate and already tense situation. We also condemn the 
attacks that led to the deaths of 4 UN Observers in Lebanon. 
India had also condemned the wholly unjustified arrest and continuing 
detention of Ministers of the Palestinian National Authority and members of 
Palestinian Legislative Council. There can be no justification whatsoever for taking 
such action against the duly elected representatives of the Palestinian people. 
Sir, the virtual destruction of a country which has been painfully rebuilt after two 
decades of civil war can hardly be countenanced by any civilized state. In response 
to the appeal issued by the Government of Lebanon, I would like to inform the 
House that the Government of India has decided to contribute Rs. 10 crores to 
humanitarian and relief efforts to rebuild Lebanon. In our view, there should 
be an immediate ceasefire so that destruction of Lebanon is ended and 
humanitarian assistance could be provided. All sides must immediately halt the 
violence and give diplomacy a chance. Diplomacy to succeed should have a 
long-term solution that involves and addresses the legitimate concerns of all 
parties in the region, leading to a comprehensive and negotiated solution. 
The safety and welfare of Indian nationals who were residents in that country 
has been our foremost concern. On 17th July, anticipating a further deterioration in 
the security situation, an advisory was issued to all Indian nationals, particularly 
those living in Sout hern Lebanon, to take suitabl e precautions regarding their 
personal safety. Consultations were initiated to work out solutions on how to 
facilitate the return on those of our nationals in Lebanon desirous of doing so. Ali 
Indian nationals have been advised to remain in contact with the Embssay of 
India in Beirut, who has been instructed to render necessary advice and 
updated information on the evolving situation. 
Since Beirut airport remained closed and the land route between Beirut and 
Damascus was unsecwred, it was felt that the best way to evacuate Indian 
nationals was through Beirut port. Four Indian Naval ships—INS Mumbai, INS 
Brahmaputra, INS Betwa and INS Shakti—which were in 
330 

[27 July, 2006] RAJYA SABHA 
the Red Sea area, were redirected to Beirut to assist in the evacuation. 
The first evacuation effort was undertaken on 21st July 2006. 598 
Indian nationals, and as a humanitarian gesture, nationals from Nepal, Lebanon, 
and Sri Lanka, were evacuated by INS Mumbai from Beirut to Larnaca in Cyprus. 
From Larnaca, Air India arranged two aircraft to ferry the evacuated Indians to 
Mumbai and Chennai. 
A second evacuation out of Beirut was undertaken on 24th July. This 
comprised 887 people, including 784 Indians, 41 from Nepal, 57 from Sri 
Lanka and 5 Lebanese nationals. All Indian nationals, and nationals from 
Nepal and Sri Lanka were air-lifted from Larnaca to India and have arrived 
safely. A third phase of evacuation was completed on 26th July bringing the total 
number of those evacuated to 1870, including 1687 Indian nationals. 
It is our estimate that approximatel y 12,000 Indian nationals were in 
Lebanon at the time of the outbreak of hostilities. They are mostly semi-skilled 
and unskilled workers who were working in farms and factories. Of these a 
large number have not indicated their desire to leave Lebanon. Some of them 
appear to have decided to stay back, others may have been unable to reach 
Beirut because of the disruption in co mmunications. We have so far received 
confirmation of the death of  one Indian national in an air strike on a glass 
factory in Bekka valley. 
Our Embassy continues to function in Beirut, and is in touch with 
various organisations and agencies with which Indian nationals were 
associated. For the time being, our naval vessels will continue to be in the 
region in case they are required to be used in the service of our nationals. Any 
further evacuations will be planned taking into account the ground situation in 
Lebanon. 
We also have a contingent of 672 Indian officers and soldiers as part of 
the UN peace-keeping forces in Lebanon (UNIFIL). Our peacekeepers are 
safe, though currently confined to their barracks. 
I would like to place on record appreciation for the efforts of various 
Ministries, Departments and agencies of Government for the swift and successful 
maner in which they have responded to the task of helping our fellow civizens in 
distress.
